title: Problem-Oriented Medical Record and SOAP Notes

sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe the problem-oriented medical record (POMR) and the role of the problem list.
- Explain the structure and purpose of the SOAP note and correctly classify information into its four sections.
- Identify who documents each part of the record and the medical office assistant's supportive documentation role.
- Apply HIPAA privacy, access, amendment, and minimum necessary principles to medical record documentation.
- Recognize documentation integrity and safety practices, including proper corrections, timeliness, and escalation of errors.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

POMR is short for a medical record that is built like a to-do list of the patient's health problems, and the P is for Problem.

### Question 2

SOAP is like a recipe with four steps in order: what you say, what we can measure, what the doctor thinks, and what we do next.

### Question 3

The problem list is like the table of contents for a patient's health book; it lists every health issue and points to the notes about each one.

### Question 4

A problem-oriented record is sorted by health problems, like sorting a messy desk into folders by topic instead of by who handed you each paper.

### Question 5

Subjective is what the patient tells you about how they feel, like telling a friend your stomach hurts.

### Question 6

Objective is the part you can measure or see with tools, like the number on a thermometer or a scale.

### Question 7

Assessment is the doctor's conclusion, like a detective naming the suspect after looking at all the clues.

### Question 8

Plan is the to-do list of next steps, like writing down exactly what chores to do after the meeting.

### Question 9

When a patient says their head hurts, that is their own report, so it goes in the Subjective pile.

### Question 10

Numbers you get from instruments, like a blood pressure cuff, are Objective facts, like a score in a game.

### Question 11

The diagnosis is the doctor's answer to the mystery, so it goes in the Assessment slot.

### Question 12

The Plan is the list of next steps, like a coach writing down the plays for the next game.

### Question 13

Only the trained doctor gets to decide the diagnosis, like only a referee can make the final call in a game.

### Question 14

The assistant is like a careful scribe who writes everything down neatly, while the doctor does the thinking.

### Question 15

Subjective is what someone tells you, and Objective is what you can see or measure for yourself.

### Question 16

SOAP goes in order like the alphabet: report first, then measure, then decide, then act.

### Question 17

A progress note is like a journal entry written after each appointment about what happened that day.

### Question 18

A complete record is like keeping careful notes so you and others can always remember exactly what happened.

### Question 19

The medical record is part of a special locked box of a patient's private health papers that only certain people may open.

### Question 20

You have the right to see and get a copy of your own health file, but not anyone else's.

### Question 21

If your health file has a mistake, you can ask the office to fix it, but you cannot make them erase things on your own.

### Question 22

The minimum necessary rule is like only taking the one file you need for your job instead of opening the whole filing cabinet.

### Question 23

Fixing a mistake is like crossing out a wrong answer in ink and writing the right one beside it, never scribbling it out so no one can see.

### Question 24

Signing and dating is like writing your name on your homework so everyone knows who did it and when.

### Question 25

Write down just the facts, like a news reporter, not your personal opinion about the person.

### Question 26

What the patient tells you about their cough goes in the Subjective box.

### Question 27

Lab numbers are Objective facts, like the score shown on a stopwatch.

### Question 28

When the doctor says what they think is wrong, that is the Assessment.

### Question 29

The Plan is the list of what to do next, like the errands written on a sticky note.

### Question 30

Taking a temperature and writing down the number is recording a fact, not deciding what is wrong.

### Question 31

Write down exactly what the patient said, like quoting a friend word for word.

### Question 32

The assistant can write down facts and measurements, but only the doctor writes down the diagnosis.

### Question 33

When a test number looks unusual, hand it to the doctor right away; do not try to explain it yourself.

### Question 34

Write down only what the person said, like taking a message for a parent without adding your own ideas.

### Question 35

Each health problem gets its own numbered folder with its own notes, like separate tabs in a binder.

### Question 36

Each health issue gets its own number on the list, like separate items on a grocery list.

### Question 37

Write down the number the patient gives, like recording the score someone reports in a game, without adding your opinion.

### Question 38

If you add a note later, label it 'added later' with the real date, like dating a journal entry honestly.

### Question 39

Leaving no blank lines is like not leaving empty space on an official form where someone could write something in later.

### Question 40

Only open the drawers you need for your job, not the whole file cabinet.

### Question 41

Locking your screen is like locking your locker before walking away so no one can look inside.

### Question 42

Private information is like a secret; you only share it where no one else can hear.

### Question 43

If a patient says something in their file is wrong, the office looks into it and either fixes it or writes down why not.

### Question 44

If you make a mistake, fix it the right way and show what you changed, like correcting your name on a form with your initials.

### Question 45

Do not rewrite someone else's answers; you can help organize, but you cannot change what the doctor wrote.

### Question 46

Writing things down right away is like writing a note while you still remember it, before you forget.

### Question 47

Use only the shortcuts everyone has agreed on, like using only the class's official abbreviations in a shared notebook.

### Question 48

Everyone uses their own locker key, not one shared key, so you always know who opened what.

### Question 49

You cannot hand out someone's private papers to a relative unless the person said it is okay.

### Question 50

Sending records is like mailing a package; you double-check the address and seal it properly.

### Question 51

Cross a finished problem off the list, but do not rip out the old pages about it.

### Question 52

Subjective is the patient's side of the story, told in their own words.

### Question 53

Objective is the facts you can see or measure, like exam findings and lab numbers.

### Question 54

The Assessment is the doctor's conclusion, the answer to what is wrong.

### Question 55

The Plan is the to-do list of treatments and next steps.

### Question 56

SOAP is like everyone using the same labeled folders, so anyone can find things fast.

### Question 57

If your writing is hard to read, someone might read the wrong word, like mistaking a 4 for a 9.

### Question 58

The assistant can write down what the patient says, but not decide what it means.

### Question 59

Taking a measurement and writing it down is recording a fact, not deciding what is wrong.

### Question 60

The designated record set is the folder of papers about a patient's care and bills that they have a right to see and fix.

### Question 61

An audit trail is like a security camera log that shows who opened the door and when.

### Question 62

Give each worker only the papers they need for their job, nothing extra.

### Question 63

The bill has to match what actually happened and what is written down, like a receipt matching the items you bought.

### Question 64

If someone sees it happen and writes it down, it is Objective, like recording that it rained because you saw it.

### Question 65

When the doctor sees the patient looks calm and comfortable, that is an observation, which is Objective.

### Question 66

Teaching the patient what to do is a next step, so it goes in the Plan.

### Question 67

The Assessment is the doctor's expert conclusion, not something the assistant writes.

### Question 68

If a patient says something in their file is wrong, the office checks it and either fixes it or writes down why they disagree, and keeps the request.

### Question 69

Something only the patient can feel and tell you, like dizziness, is Subjective.

### Question 70

If you put a paper in the wrong folder, tell someone right away and fix it properly instead of hiding it.

### Question 71

Only the doctor writes the diagnosis; the assistant can help write down what is dictated but not decide it.

### Question 72

Send only the papers needed for the request, like mailing only the one form someone asked for.

### Question 73

If you lose something important, tell an adult in charge right away, not later and not by shouting it in public.

### Question 74

Type exactly what the doctor says, like writing down a story word for word without making up parts.

### Question 75

The problem list is like a labeled map of the patient's health that any new doctor can read quickly.

### Question 76

An addendum is like adding a dated postscript to a letter instead of erasing what was already written.

### Question 77

When you are not sure if you are allowed to do something, ask the person in charge first.

### Question 78

Match each piece to its SOAP slot: what they said, what we measured, what the doctor thinks, and what we do next.

### Question 79

De-identified data is like a paper with the name cut off, so it cannot be traced to a person; the designated record set is the full folder with the name still on it.

### Question 80

If a sentence is missing a word, ask the author what it should say instead of making it up.

### Question 81

Only the doctor can change the diagnosis, so the assistant helps the patient make a formal request instead of changing it personally.

### Question 82

Shared computer? Everyone uses their own key and locks the door when they leave.

### Question 83

A note with a person's name and health details is private, like a diary, and must be kept locked up.

### Question 84

If you spot a mistake that could hurt someone, speak up right away instead of staying quiet.

### Question 85

A new health issue gets its own new folder and its own notes, added to the others without throwing any away.
